Race is a significant aspect of identity, but it is not entirely self-determined. Most individuals are socially assigned a race primarily based on their appearance. Scientifically, the only difference in skin color is due to melanin, yet it has historically been exploited for more harmful purposes.

There have been significant shortcomings in race-based medical care. Individuals from various Asian backgrounds, in particular, have faced challenges due to the diversity within that racial category. For instance, Asian Americans generally exhibit the lowest rates of obesity and related health issues. East Asians tend to be socioeconomically better off than Southeast Asians, resulting in notably lower rates of obesity, heart disease, and diabetes. In fact, certain groups, such as those from specific Southeast Asian countries, experience higher rates of these conditions compared to Black or Latino populations in the country. Because the largest Asian demographics in the country are of Chinese descent, race can negatively impact the medical treatment of smaller Asian groups, as their healthcare often differs from those with greater overall wealth.

Much of the medical science related to race focuses on ethnicity and culture, tailoring treatment based on diet, socioeconomic status, and medical sensitivities.

While we categorize race based on skin color, this classification is quite loose. Historically, even biased scientists in the early 20th century acknowledged that skin color was not a definitive factor in determining someone's race for citizenship. One notable case even altered the definition of "white" to include individuals from the Middle East, who had traditionally been classified as Asian due to darker skin, after a man from that region argued in court that he shared a geographical background with a significant historical figure. Similar shifts have occurred with groups such as the Irish and Italians being recognized as white, while individuals from the Indian subcontinent have fluctuated between classifications of white and Asian.

Race tells us to view human differences and determines societal definitions from them.

Ethnic traits are not genetically passed down, but what we consider specific ethnic features are. Parents of a certain ethnicity may have distinct hair and eye characteristics that will be inherited. However, if those parents move to a different country, what isn't passed down to their child is the cultural practices, languages, etc. Those are learned behaviors.

Now back on the symbol being used: socially, we look at distinct hair and eye characteristics and we determine those features mean the person belongs to that ethnicity. More deeply, we then associate the meanings behind how individuals from that ethnicity are viewed socially.

The university is a rough representation of a major city in Southern California. It's located in a valley that is somewhat distant from the entertainment district, downtown area, coastal attractions, and other nearby cities. You'll definitely need a vehicle if you want to feel like a true local.

The dormitories themselves are decent. However, the meal plans leave much to be desired. The food quality is poor, and the residence halls are closed during breaks like winter. You can opt for a double apartment with a kitchen, allowing you to prepare your own meals.

The campus is quite pleasant. People are generally friendly. Students may come off as a bit bitter and disillusioned, but they are usually approachable and willing to help. The faculty varies; lower division instructors often lack enthusiasm, as many teach part-time at community colleges and treat their role at this university similarly. In contrast, upper division professors tend to be quite knowledgeable, and many maintain friendships with students after graduation.

If you're looking to experience life in a major city, this university offers an affordable, low-risk option, though you will need to make an effort to explore the city's offerings. The student body is likely the best representation of the local community, featuring a diverse mix of primarily working-class individuals, many of whom juggle multiple jobs. While it may not be as prestigious as other nearby institutions, it provides a unique experience.

In this study, women engineers from a specific ethnic background were significantly more likely than their white counterparts to report being held to higher standards than their colleagues. Taken more broadly, this suggests a pernicious bind: Though individuals from this ethnic group might be seen as having a specific set of technical skills, white men with identical skills may be assumed to have a broader range of skills they haven’t demonstrated. So, like women and other people of color, individuals from this ethnic group in STEM may have to be more skilled than white men to be seen as equally competent.

This is a very good way of understanding the difference between white and candidates from this ethnic background. Terms such as "more well-rounded" and "more than just an employee" are terms that often excuse picking over a candidate from a different background.
